docs.text: A newsletter or a promotion is more than one email: it has an audience, a goal, a send date and results you will want to compare with the next one. Running it as a tactic inside a campaign keeps all of that together, and the results feed the campaign report.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A mailing list or a segment to send to. See Mailing lists and Contacts.
  • An email design with your brand, so you only write the content. See Emails.
  • Your email sending set up under Connections. Until it is, the tactic shows You need to setup your email provider.

docs.title: 1. Set up the campaign
docs.text:
1. Choose Marketing → Campaigns, then Create New Campaign (or open an existing one).
  2. Fill in the objective, dates, audience and description. The description is what the AI reads when it writes for this campaign, so say who you target and what you offer.

See Campaigns.

docs.title: 2. Add the email tactic
docs.text:
1. In the campaign, under Tactics, choose Add Tactic and pick Email Campaign.
  2. Give it a name and a Send date.

docs.title: 3. Write the email
docs.text:
1. Open the tactic. Under Email Management, choose Add Email: create a new one, or pick one from your Email Gallery.
  2. Write it in the editor, or let the AI draft it from the campaign's description. To greet each recipient by name, type {{contact_firstname}} where the name should go; see Personalising an email.

  3. Under Subject & sender, set the subject and who it comes from for this send. Leave a field blank to use the email's own value or your default.

  4. Under Recipients, choose the mailing list or segment.

docs.title: 4. Test, then send or schedule
docs.text:
1. Send yourself a test and check it on your phone and in Gmail or Outlook.
  2. Send now, or let it go at the send date. The email shows Published with the date once it is out.
  3. To reach more people later, for example contacts who joined the list since, use Send To More People.

docs.title: 5. Read the results
docs.text:
The tactic's Performance panel shows how the email did:

  • Sent, Delivered, Unique Opens, Unique Clicks, Bounced and Unsubscribed, each with its rate.
  • Activity Over Time: opens and clicks day by day after the send.
  • Email Funnel: from sent to clicked, where people dropped off.

Opens by mail-provider robots and security scanners are left out, so the open rate reflects people. Turn on Include machine & bot activity to see everything.

Below the funnel:

  • Who opened and clicked separates real people from Apple Mail Privacy Protection, which opens every email automatically and is filtered out of your open rate. Opens by device shows mobile, desktop and tablet.

  • Recipients: each recipient with whether the email was sent, delivered, opened and clicked. Search by email or name, and Export CSV for your own analysis.

  • Link Performance: each link with its total clicks, clicks by known contacts, unique clickers and anonymous clicks. Clickers lists who clicked a link: a ready-made list of interested people.

  • Details: every count in one table: sent, delivered, opens, clicks, bounces, errors and unsubscribes.

The same figures appear in the campaign's Analytics tab, next to the other tactics. See The campaign report.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Only subscribed contacts are emailed. Contacts who unsubscribed, or never gave consent, are left out of the send automatically.
  • A tactic sends one email. For a reminder or a follow-up, add another email tactic to the same campaign; each keeps its own results.
  • Compare like with like. Open rates vary with the list and the day; compare this email with earlier sends to the same list.

docs.title: Improve your presence with SEO
docs.text:
Get found by people searching for what you do, in Google and in AI assistants, and see the effect of your work in clicks.

This guide follows one loop: see where you stand, fix the pages that matter, write what your market searches for, and measure. Count about an hour to set up, then a regular hour a week.

docs.title: 1. Connect your site
docs.text:
Under Settings → Connections, connect Google Search Console for your website, and Google Analytics. Search Console gives clicks, impressions and positions; Analytics says what visitors did once they arrived.

See Connections.

Check the connection

If a screen stays empty, open Organic Visibility → Performance & Report → Diagnostics: it shows which site and property every screen reads, and whether each Google connection answers.

docs.title: 2. See where you stand
docs.text:
Open Organic Visibility → Performance & Report. Note four numbers for the last 28 days: clicks, impressions, average position and click rate, and whether the trend goes up or down.

This is your starting point. The Executive Report tab puts it on one page for your manager.

See Performance & Report.

docs.title: 3. Fix the pages that matter most
docs.text:
Open Organic Visibility → Page Fixes. The pages are ranked by the clicks a fix could bring. Start with Low CTR: pages people see but do not click. A better title and description take minutes.

Choose Add To Queue on the fixes you will do. They land in Actions, with the steps, so the work is tracked until it is verified.

See Page Fixes and Actions.

docs.title: 4. Write what your market searches for
docs.text:
Open Content Hub → Research & Plan. The topics are ranked from your own data: searches you could win, questions people ask, gaps against your competitors. Pick one with steady searches and low competition.

Write it in the Content Workspace: the AI writer drafts it in your brand voice from the topic's data, the reviewer scores it, and you revise until it is ready. Publish it on your site.

See Research & Plan and Content Workspace.

docs.title: 5. Make sure AI assistants can quote you
docs.text:
Open Organic Visibility → AI Readiness & Authority. The score shows whether assistants such as ChatGPT or Gemini can read and trust your pages. The lowest pillar is usually Answers & FAQ: add the questions your customers really ask, with short answers.

See AI Readiness & Authority.

docs.title: 6. Measure, a few weeks later
docs.text:
Search results take two to six weeks to react. Come back to Performance & Report:

  • Impact shows what your shipped work actually changed.
  • Content Hub → Momentum shows the pages rising right now: give them a push while the trend is with you, for example in your next newsletter.

See Momentum.

docs.title: Your weekly hour
docs.text:
1. Performance & Report: the four numbers, and any pattern detected.
  2. Page Fixes: add the top one or two to the queue.
  3. Actions: finish what is in progress.
  4. Momentum: push one rising page.
  5. Research & Plan: write one new piece a week or two.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Position going down is good. Position 1 is the top of the results.
  • Do not judge a change after a few days. Search Console data is two to three days behind, and rankings move slowly.
  • One good page beats five thin ones. Write fewer pieces, each answering a real search fully.

docs.title: Run an event from start to finish
docs.text: From the first invitation to the thank-you email: everything an in-person, online or hybrid event needs, in the order you will do it. Allow about an hour to set up your first event; later ones go faster because you can duplicate them.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: An event touches every part of your marketing: your audience, a landing page, a registration form, several emails, check-in at the door and the follow-up. GoodBards keeps all of it on one event page, and every guest who registers becomes a contact you can market to afterwards.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Your Brand Kit, so the landing page and emails look like you. See Brand Kit.
  • The people you will invite, as a segment or a mailing list. See Contacts.

docs.title: 1. Create the event
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Event Management. Your events are listed as cards, with their status, date, place and registrations.

  2. Choose New Event, then give it a name, a date and time, and a place.

  3. Open the event. It starts on the Overview: registrations against capacity, invitations sent, days to go, and quick actions such as Copy Registration Link. The tabs follow the life of the event, from left to right.

The dots on a tab show it is set up. Everything saves on its own: there is no Save button on the event page.

docs.title: 2. Describe the event
docs.text:
On the Definition tab:

  1. Set the Event Type, the Format (in person, online or hybrid) and the Visibility.

  2. Under About the event, write a Short Description, the Address, and choose a Cover Image. These appear on the landing page and in every email.

  3. For an online or hybrid event, add the Join link. Only confirmed guests receive it.

The event's name, date and place in every email come from this tab. To change them, change them here, never inside an email.

The Landing page tab shows the page guests register on, built from what you just wrote. To change its layout, choose Duplicate to customize.

docs.title: 3. Prepare the registration
docs.text:
On the Registration tab:

  1. Under Settings, set the Max Capacity, when registration opens and closes, and whether to Require Approval.

  2. Turn on the Waitlist if the event can fill up, and choose how a freed seat is given: Automatic (the next person in line is seated and emailed) or Manual (you choose).

  3. The blocks below are folded; click a title to open one.

  4. Under Registration form, keep the default form (name, email, company, job title) or choose one of your own. See Forms.

  5. Under Contact registration, check which form fields fill in the contact: email, first and last name, and anything else you want to keep with Add Mapping. Changes save on their own.

docs.title: 4. Set up the emails
docs.text:
Each guest receives the right email for their situation automatically. Under Registration emails, the list shows the emails your event can send, and grows when you turn on approval or the waitlist.

To change one:

  1. Open it and choose Edit on the preview.
  2. Change the Subject at the top and the text in the editor, then choose Apply.

The invitation and the reminders work the same way, on the Communications tab. See Editing an email.

docs.title: 5. Invite your audience
docs.text:
1. On the Communications tab, under Invitation email, choose the audience to invite.
  2. Choose Send Invitations. You can also send them from the Actions menu.
  3. Add Registration reminders for people who have not registered yet, and Event reminders for guests, for example one day and one hour before.

At the bottom of the tab, Sent emails lists every email the event has sent, with the number of recipients.

docs.title: Promote it on social media
docs.text:
On the Overview tab, Promote On Social writes the event's posts for you: the announcement, a reminder, a last call and a happening today post, from the event's own facts and with its cover image, for the social channels of the campaign.

The posts arrive as drafts on the campaign's social tactics, each with a suggested date counted back from the event. Nothing is published until you schedule it. The button is not available for private events or events without a date. See also Social Post.

docs.title: Show your events on your website
docs.text: In Marketing → Event Management, the menu at the top right offers Open public page (the page listing all your public events) and Embed form. The embed gives you a code to paste into your website, with a light, dark or automatic theme and a list or grid layout, so visitors see and register for your events without leaving your site.

docs.title: 6. Manage registrations
docs.text:
The Attendance tab lists every guest, their status and the last email they received.

  • Approve or decline requests when approval is on.
  • ↑ Promote a waiting guest when the waitlist is in Manual mode.
  • Add Attendee to register someone yourself, for example from a phone call.
  • The eye icon opens a guest's history with this event: what was sent, delivered, opened and clicked. Useful when a guest says they never got their confirmation.

docs.title: 7. On the day
docs.text:
Every confirmed guest has a QR code in their confirmation and reminder emails.

  1. Open the Actions menu.
  2. Choose Scan attendee to check guests in with your phone or laptop camera, or Kiosk mode to let them check themselves in at the entrance.

  3. To print name badges, set the format under Attendance → Badge, then use the print icon on a guest's row.

See Check-in and badges for the details.

docs.title: 8. Follow up
docs.text:
1. When the event is over, choose Actions → End event. Guests who were not checked in are marked as absent.
  2. On the Follow-up tab, set the email for those who attended, those who did not, and those you invited who never registered. Attach a survey form if you want feedback.

  3. On the Analytics tab, see registrations broken down by status or by any form field, and choose Email Performance to see how every event email did.

  4. If you attached a survey to the follow-up, its answers appear on the Follow-up tab as charts per question, with a CSV download.

docs.title: Cancelling an event
docs.text: Actions → Cancel event cancels it. Every registered guest is emailed that the event is cancelled, and it cannot be undone. To stop new registrations but keep the event, use Close registration instead.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Publish before you share the link. A draft event does not accept registrations.
  • Cancel a registration with ⊘, not with the status menu. ⊘ emails the guest and offers the seat to the waitlist; the status menu only corrects the list.
  • Every guest becomes a contact. After the event, find them in your audience and follow up with a normal email or campaign.
  • Next time, duplicate. Duplicating an event copies its settings, emails and form, so only the date and details change.

docs.title: Run a campaign on social media
docs.text: Plan a series of posts around one goal, write them in your brand voice, schedule them across your networks, and see what worked.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: One post rarely moves anything; a series does. Running your posts as tactics of a campaign keeps the whole series, per network, on one calendar, and puts the results next to your emails, events and ads in the campaign report.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Your social accounts connected: LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram or X. See Connections.
  • Your Brand Kit and, if you have one, a Brand Voice, so the AI writes like you. See How the AI knows your brand.

docs.title: 1. Set up the campaign
docs.text:
1. Choose Marketing → Campaigns, then Create New Campaign.
  2. Fill in the objective, dates, audience, regions and description.
  3. Under Tactics, choose Plan With AI to get a suggested mix of tactics for your objective, or Add Tactic to add one per network yourself, for example Instagram: gift guide reels and LinkedIn: corporate gifting.

See Campaigns.

docs.title: 2. Write the posts
docs.text:
For each network:

  1. Choose Write Content With AI on the campaign, or write a post in Social Media → Social Post with New Post.
  2. Check the text, add an image, and use AI Hashtags and Improve With AI. The preview shows the post as it will appear on the network.
  3. To turn an article into a series of posts in one go, open the article in Content Hub → Content Repository and choose Create social posts.

See Social Post.

docs.title: 3. Schedule them
docs.text:
1. Open the network's tactic. Under Asset Management, choose Import Asset to add your posts, or Link Published Post for a post you already published on the network yourself.

  2. Give each post its date and time. The list shows each one as Scheduled or Published, with its destination account.

  3. Check the whole series on the campaign's Calendar tab: every post, email and event of the campaign, by week, month or year.

docs.title: 4. See what worked
docs.text:
• Per network: Social Media → Analysis shows reach, engagement, likes, comments, shares and clicks, and the sentiment of the reactions. See Analysis.
  • For the whole campaign: the campaign's Analytics tab adds up every tactic. See The campaign report.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Post dates must fall within the campaign's dates. Change the campaign's dates under Campaign Details if you need to extend it.
  • Each network has its own format and limit. Write one post per network; the editor shows each network's character limit and preview.
  • Results are not live. Network figures are collected several times a day, so a post's first results appear a few hours after it is published.

docs.title: Use GoodBards from your AI assistant (MCP)
Use GoodBards from your AI assistant (MCP)
docs.text: Work with GoodBards from the AI assistant you already use, such as Claude: ask your GoodBards agents to write or research, read your social and campaign reports, without opening GoodBards.

docs.title: What MCP is
docs.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for an AI assistant to use outside tools. GoodBards offers an MCP server: once your assistant is connected, it can call GoodBards' tools for you, with your company's brand and data.

docs.title: What your assistant can do
docs.text:
What it can do depends on the permissions (scopes) you grant when you connect:

Permission Tools agents:invoke (always) List your GoodBards agents, and ask one to write, research or analyse. reports:read Read your social accounts and reports, Google Analytics reports, campaigns and content. reports:write Start a new social report. content:write Save a new piece of content, and schedule a post.

Grant only what you need. With agents:invoke alone, the assistant can talk to your agents but cannot read reports or create content.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the connection in GoodBards
docs.text:
A company administrator does this once.

  1. Open Tenant Settings → Security, and create an API key for the assistant. See Use the GoodBards API.
  2. On that key, choose OAuth Apps, then Create OAuth App. Give it a name, for example Claude AI Connector.
  3. Copy the Client ID and the Client Secret. The secret is shown only once.

docs.title: 2. Connect your assistant
docs.text:
In your assistant's connector settings (in Claude: Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector):

Setting Value Server URL https://mcp.goodbards.ai/mcp Client ID From step 1 Client Secret From step 1

The assistant opens a GoodBards page asking you to Allow the access. Once you allow it, the tools appear in your assistant.

Developers can instead send the API key directly, as Authorization: Bearer <your API key>; the assistant then gets the agent tools only.

docs.title: 3. Use your agents
docs.text:
Ask in plain words, for example:

  • "List my GoodBards agents."
  • "Ask the Brand Marketing Agent for three LinkedIn post ideas about our festive gifting guide."
  • "Get the latest LinkedIn report for Tropika Home and summarise it."

To continue a conversation with the same agent, keep asking in the same chat: the assistant reuses the session.

docs.title: 4. Stay in control
docs.text:
• Everything happens in your company. The connection belongs to one company and acts as the administrator who created the OAuth app.
  • Check before anything is saved or scheduled. With content:write, ask the assistant to show you the content before it saves it or schedules a post.
  • Disconnect at any time: delete the OAuth app, or revoke the API key, on the Security tab. The assistant loses access straight away.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Access tokens last an hour and renew on their own for up to 30 days; after that, allow the access again.
  • Your agents work as in GoodBards, with your brand voice and knowledge, and their usage counts toward your plan.

docs.title: Use the GoodBards API
docs.text:
Connect your own tools to GoodBards: push contacts from your website or CRM, and pull campaigns and results into your own reports.

This guide is for the developer who writes the connection. It takes about an hour for a first call.

docs.title: 1. Create an API key
docs.text:
Only a company administrator can create keys.

  1. Open Tenant Settings from your account menu, then the Security tab.
  2. Under API Keys, choose Create API Key.

  3. Fill in:

    Field What to put Description What the key is for, for example Website sign-up form. Scope FULL for the API, or CHATBOT for a key that only drives the website chatbot. Restrict to a specific origin For a key used from a web page: the only website allowed to use it. Expires at When the key stops working. Without a date, it lasts five years.

  4. Choose Generate key and copy it into your tool's secret store.

The number of keys your plan allows is shown above the list.

Treat the key like a password

A FULL key reaches all of your company's data through the API, whoever created it. Keep it on a server, never in a web page or a mobile app, and give each integration its own key so you can revoke one without breaking the others.

docs.title: 2. Authenticate your requests
docs.text:
Send the key in the Authorization header:

GET https://api.goodbards.ai/v1/{tenant-id}/campaigns
Authorization: Bearer <your API key>

Every path starts with /v1/ and your company's tenant ID. Ask support for it if you do not have it.

docs.title: Add a contact
docs.text:
POST https://api.goodbards.ai/v1/{tenant-id}/cdp/contacts/
Authorization: Bearer <your API key>
Content-Type: application/json

Update an existing contact with PUT /v1/{tenant-id}/cdp/contacts/{contact-id}. A contact sent without a status is added as subscribed: always send a status for people who did not agree to receive marketing emails. Only contacts with marketing consent should be subscribed; see Adding contacts.

docs.title: List your campaigns
docs.text: GET https://api.goodbards.ai/v1/{tenant-id}/campaigns

docs.title: Read a campaign's results
docs.text: Call What it does GET /v1/{tenant-id}/campaigns/{campaign-id}/analytics/reports Lists the campaign's reports. GET /v1/{tenant-id}/campaigns/{campaign-id}/analytics/reports/{report-id} Reads one report. POST /v1/{tenant-id}/campaigns/{campaign-id}/analytics/reports Starts a new report. It answers 202 at once; read it a little later.

docs.title: 4. Errors
docs.text:
Errors come back with an HTTP status and a JSON body:

{
  "code": "CONTACT_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "Contact not found",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-11T09:30:00"
}
Status Usually means 400 Something in the request is missing or invalid; code says what. 401 The key is missing, wrong, revoked or expired. 403 The key may not do this, or a plan limit is reached. 404 The contact, campaign or report does not exist in your company. 409 The request conflicts with the current state, for example an email already used. 5xx Our side. Retry later; if it persists, contact support with the time of the call.

docs.title: 5. Revoke a key
docs.text: On the same Security tab, open the key's menu and revoke it. Calls with that key fail with 401 straight away.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• One key per integration. A leaked key is then one key to revoke.
  • Set an expiry date and put a reminder in your calendar to renew it.
  • The full reference of endpoints is available on request from support.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Your starting point each day: what changed, what needs doing, and what is coming up.

Who sees it: everyone your administrator gives the Home access to.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Your dashboard. The Daily Pulse sums up the last day for your company: upcoming events and yesterday's registrations, how your contacts engaged, and your readiness and engagement scores with their trend. Each card links to the screen where you can act on it.

See Home and the Daily Pulse.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Your to-do list, filled by GoodBards. Each daily check (website, emails, social, events) turns what it finds into an action with the evidence and the expected impact. Work through them, mark them done, or dismiss what does not apply; done actions are measured afterwards so you can see what paid off.

See Actions.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text:
Everything scheduled in one place: campaign tactics, social posts, emails and events, by day, week or month.

See Calendar.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: Open Home each morning, then Actions. If Actions is empty, the daily checks have not found anything yet; connect your website and social accounts under Connections to give them something to read.

docs.title: Home and the Daily Pulse
docs.text: Your dashboard: everything that moved since yesterday, on one screen, with a link to act on each part.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Marketing data is spread across your website, social networks, ads, emails, events and contacts. The Daily Pulse on Home sums all of it up every morning, so you see in a minute what changed and where to look, instead of opening ten screens.

docs.title: How to read your Home
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Home. It opens on Marketing OS.
  2. At the top: Actions assigned to you, and the Workspace health (how many services are connected, how complete your company context is, how much AI credit is used).
  3. Active initiatives: your running Campaigns, the Events open for registration, and Digital Ads spend and results.
  1. Global performance: website traffic (Web Analytics), Social Media engagement per network, and Search Performance from Google Search Console.
  2. Audience & CDP: your contacts and companies, how many engaged yesterday, and your database health and engagement scores.

Each card shows the change against the previous period, with a small trend chart. Click a card to open the screen behind it; suggested action links take you straight to the matching item in Actions.

docs.title: Ask an agent
docs.text: The Agent tab, next to Marketing OS, opens a chat with your AI agents. Ask anything, add Sources or Attachments, or pick one of the suggested agents. See Chat Agents.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The pulse runs once a day. Choose Re-Run Report to refresh it now, for example after connecting a new service.
  • Cards appear when there is something to show. A card for a service you have not connected stays empty; connect it under Connections.
  • Dates on each card say how fresh it is: Today, Yesterday, or the date of the latest report.
  • The pulse can come to you by email. It is sent each morning to the colleagues who have the Recipient for daily report emails permission, and to nobody else. See Additional permissions.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Marketing
docs.text:
Plan your campaigns and launch the tactics your audience actually sees.

Who sees it: everyone your administrator gives the Marketing access to. Emails, forms, events and digital ads also sit under Marketing in the sidebar; each has its own access and its own section in these docs: Emails & Forms, Events, Digital Ads.

docs.title: Launch a Tactic
docs.text:
Publish one thing (a post, an email, an event) without setting up a campaign first. The AI suggests the tactics that fit your goal, with a score for each.

See Launch a Tactic.

docs.title: Campaigns
docs.text:
Group related tactics under one goal, with dates, a budget and a report of what each tactic brought.

See Campaigns.

docs.title: Campaign report
docs.text:
Results across every tactic of a campaign: emails, social posts, events and ads side by side.

See The campaign report.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: Read Launch a Tactic first. It explains the difference between a tactic and a campaign, which the rest of this section builds on.

docs.title: Campaigns
docs.text: Group related marketing activity under one plan, with a shared objective and a start and end date.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A campaign is a container for everything you are doing towards one goal — a product launch, an event, a seasonal push. Instead of tracking a dozen separate posts and emails, you see them together and track whether the goal is being met.

If you only want to publish one post or one email, you do not need a campaign. Use Launch a Tactic instead.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Know your objective — for example Product Launch, Brand Awareness, or Networking With Industry Professionals. You choose one when you create the campaign.
  • Know roughly when the campaign should start and finish.

docs.title: How to create a campaign
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Campaigns.
  2. Choose + Create New Campaign.
  3. Give it a name, pick an objective, and set the start and end dates.
  4. Add the tactics that belong to it — the posts, emails and events that work towards the objective.

docs.title: Reading the campaign list
docs.text:
The four tiles across the top summarise where things stand: Total, Active, Pending and Completed Campaigns.

Each row in the table shows the campaign's objective, its status, and the dates it runs between. Sort by any column using the arrows beside the heading.

Status What it means Pending Created, but not started yet. Active Currently running. Ended Finished.

docs.title: Inside a campaign
docs.text:
Click a campaign's name to open it. Its tabs are Overview, Budget, Calendar and Analytics.

Overview shows the Campaign Details: objective, budget, target industry, audience, regions, and a description the AI uses as context whenever it writes for this campaign. Choose the pencil to change them.

Below, Tactics lists everything the campaign runs: ads, blog posts, social posts, emails and events, each with its status and end date.

  • Add Tactic adds one yourself.
  • Plan With AI suggests the tactics that fit the campaign's objective.
  • Write Content With AI drafts the content of the tactics.

docs.title: Duplicating a tactic
docs.text:
To run a tactic again, for example last year's festive email, choose Duplicate in the tactic's menu. Give the copy a name and a destination campaign (the same one or another). The copy starts as a draft: dates, status and figures are reset; budget, description and audience are kept.

For its emails and content, choose:

  • Reuse existing assets: the copy uses the same emails and posts. Editing them later changes both tactics.
  • Create new copies: fresh copies, so the original is never touched.

For an event, its settings are copied too, and its registration form is always duplicated so the two events keep their registrations apart.

The copy gets its own tactic code (the original's code followed by -copy), so Google Analytics never mixes the two tactics.

docs.title: Reading a social tactic's results
docs.text:
Once a LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, X or TikTok post is published, the tactic shows a Performance by post card under its posts, with one colour per post in every chart:

  • Link clicks: people who opened the links in each post.
  • Reach & Visibility: impressions of each post.
  • Engagement Trends: clicks, likes, shares or comments of each post.

Reach and engagement are the network's figures, collected by the daily report: running totals since publication, so a post appears the day after it is published. Pick Since publish, 7, 30 or 90 days above the charts, and click a post's name to open its analytics. The same card appears when you open the tactic from the campaign's Analytics tab, where the campaign charts keep one colour per tactic.

View analytics in a published post's menu opens the same view for one post:

  • Link clicks (tracked): people who opened the links in the post, day by day, and how many clicks each link got.
  • The network's own figures for the post (impressions, reactions, comments, shares…), from the latest daily report. They appear the day after publishing.

Good to know:

  • "Clicks on LinkedIn" is a different number. The network counts every click on the post (image, "see more", profile); link clicks count only the people who opened your links.
  • Bots are left out. When a post is published, the network fetches its links to build the preview card; those visits are not counted. Switch on Include bots to see them.
  • Days follow your timezone.
  • A post linked from outside GoodBards has no tracked links: it shows the network figures only.

docs.title: Tracking links in Google Analytics
docs.text:
Every link GoodBards shortens in a campaign's emails and social posts carries UTM tags, so its visits show up in your Google Analytics reports:

Tag Value Example utm_campaign the campaign code summer-sale-2026 utm_content the tactic code: tells two tactics of the same campaign apart launch-post utm_source where the click comes from, set from the tactic type linkedin, facebook, newsletter for emails, event for event emails utm_medium the channel family, set from the tactic type social or email
  • The codes are optional. Leave them empty and GoodBards writes one from the name ("Summer Sale 2026" becomes summer-sale-2026) and keeps it, even if you rename the campaign later.
  • Format: lowercase letters, digits, - and _, up to 50 characters. A campaign code is unique in your workspace, a tactic code within its campaign.
  • Source and medium can't be edited, so every campaign is named the same way in your reports. The tactic form shows the tags its links get.
  • Your own tags win. A link that already contains utm_ tags is left as you wrote it.
  • Ads and blog posts get no tags: Google Ads tags its own clicks, and tags on links to your own website would overwrite your visitors' real source.

docs.title: The Budget tab
docs.text:
The Budget tab splits the campaign's budget across its tactics. On the left, how much is used of the total, with the remaining amount, the amount Allocated (choose the pencil to change it) and the average per tactic. On the right, every tactic with its own budget; choose the pencil on a row to change it.

A red mark next to a tactic's budget means it is above the average budget per tactic. The tactic budgets are your plan. For ads, Google Ads spends its own daily budget; see Ads in a campaign.

docs.title: The campaign report
docs.text:
The Analytics tab gathers the results of every tactic in one place: reach and engagement on social networks, email deliveries, opens and clicks, event registrations and attendance, and ad spend and returns. Each figure shows its change against the previous report. Use the arrows to move between report dates, or History to see them all.

Below the totals, a table lists every tactic with its own figures. Choose one to open its details: the same figures for that tactic alone, and its share of the campaign total.

docs.title: Starting and stopping
docs.text:
The Start / Stop column controls whether a campaign is running:

  • ▶ Start begins a pending campaign.
  • ⏸ Pause stops an active one.

Pausing does not delete anything — it stops further activity until you start it again.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A campaign is a plan, not a channel. Publishing still happens through the individual tactics inside it.
  • Name campaigns so you can find them later. Something like Q4-2026-Product-Launch is easier to search than New campaign.
  • End dates are not deadlines. A campaign past its end date stays visible in the list; the date describes the plan, it does not stop work by itself.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Digital Ads
docs.text: Manage your paid advertising — campaigns, keywords, conversion tracking and reporting — without leaving GoodBards.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Paid advertising is where marketing budget turns into traffic, and where it disappears fastest if nobody is watching. This brings your ad campaigns and their performance in beside the rest of your marketing, so spend can be judged against everything else you are doing.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Your Google Ads account must be connected. See Connections.

Google Ads today; Meta and LinkedIn to follow

Google Ads is available now. Meta Ads and LinkedIn Ads appear marked Soon and cannot be used yet.

docs.title: Getting your first campaign live
docs.text:
New campaigns do not start spending on their own. The three steps are:

  1. Create a campaign — on the Campaigns tab, launch a Search campaign with its daily budget. New campaigns start paused.
  2. Add ad groups & keywords — structure the campaign and choose the searches you want to appear for.
  3. Enable it to go live — a campaign needs at least one enabled ad. Enabling it is the moment spend starts.

docs.title: Creating a campaign
docs.text:
On the Campaigns tab, choose New Campaign. The wizard has four steps, and Google checks the campaign before anything is created:

  1. Basics: the name, the objective (Sales, Leads or Traffic) and the channel. The bidding follows from the objective.

  2. Budget & schedule: the daily budget, and optional start and end dates.

  3. Keywords & targeting: the searches to appear for, the locations and the language (see below).
  4. Review: check everything, then create. The campaign starts paused.

docs.title: Choosing keywords
docs.text:
Step 3 offers five ways to find keywords:

Source What it gives you Search Console The searches that already bring people to your site. Keyword Planner Ideas from Google, with monthly searches, competition and the top-of-page bid. CSV upload Your own list, from a spreadsheet. Competitors Ideas taken from a competitor's website. Manual Type them yourself.

In Keyword Planner, type a few seed keywords separated by commas and search. Choose + to add an idea to the campaign.

Volumes are worldwide until you set Locations and Language; search again afterwards for local demand, for example Singapore only.

Nothing spends until you enable it

A campaign sitting at zero spend is usually paused rather than broken. That is deliberate — it stops half-built campaigns burning budget. Check the campaign is enabled and has at least one enabled ad.

docs.title: Reading the overview
docs.text:
Set the period with the date selector, then read the four headline figures:

Metric What it means Total spend What you have spent, in your account currency. Conversions How many people did the thing you were paying for. Blended ROAS Return on ad spend — revenue divided by spend. 2.00x means two dollars back for every one spent. CTR Click-through rate: the share of people who clicked after seeing your ad.

ROAS is the number that decides whether a campaign continues. CTR tells you whether the ad itself is working — a low CTR usually means the ad copy or the keywords are wrong, not the budget.

Below, Spend by channel shows daily spend stacked by channel, and Budget allocation shows how spend is split across campaigns.

docs.title: Managing a campaign
docs.text:
On the Campaigns tab, choose a campaign to open its panel.

  • Overview: its performance and spend over the period, and what stops it from serving, for example no ad groups or an ad group with no ads. Change the name, daily budget and dates; changes apply immediately in Google Ads. Enable starts serving and spending; Remove is permanent in Google Ads.
  • Ad groups: each group's Keywords and Ads. New ads start paused. An ad's text, and a keyword's text and match type, cannot be changed once created: pause it and add a corrected one.
  • Negatives: searches the campaign must not show on, for example free or jobs. A single ad group can also have its own negative keywords; the two lists are independent.

Video campaigns are managed in Google Ads itself: GoodBards shows their performance but cannot edit them.

docs.title: Ads in a campaign
docs.text:
To count an ad campaign in a marketing campaign's results, add an Ads tactic to the marketing campaign, open it, and pick the Google Ads campaign to link it to. The tactic then shows the ad campaign's last 30 days: spend and results.

Two budgets appear side by side on purpose: the tactic budget is what you planned for this tactic in the marketing campaign; the daily budget is what Google Ads spends. Neither changes the other. To create the Google Ads campaign itself, use Marketing → Digital Ads; the tactic only links to it. Unlink removes the link without touching the ad campaign.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Google's own suggestions for your account. You can apply keyword recommendations: they add keywords within your existing budget and bidding. Budget and bidding suggestions can only be dismissed here; handle them in Google Ads if you want them.

Applying cannot be undone, and a dismissed suggestion may come back later. When Google has nothing to suggest, the tab says All caught up.

docs.title: Conversion Tracking
docs.text:
What counts as a result for your ads: a purchase, a lead form sent. Without it, conversions and ROAS stay at zero.

  • New Conversion Action creates one.
  • The code icon shows the tag to put on your website for that conversion.
  • Actions imported from Google Analytics need no tag: Google Analytics already tracks them.

docs.title: Callouts
docs.text: Short extra lines shown with your ads across all campaigns, such as Free shipping or 24/7 support, up to 25 characters each. Type one and choose Add Callout.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• Automation policy: nothing in Digital Ads acts on its own. Every action that can affect spend (enabling a campaign, changing a budget, creating an ad, applying a recommendation) asks for your confirmation.
  • AI grounding: the brand data the AI uses to prefill campaigns and draft ad copy. Without a tone of voice, ad copy is not matched to your voice; choose Edit In Company Settings to add one.
  • Audit trail: every real change made to Google Ads through GoodBards, newest first. Filter it by kind of action.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Conversion tracking first. Without it, ROAS and conversions stay at zero and you are flying blind. Set it up before spending.
  • Start with a small daily budget. Raise it once you can see which keywords convert. It is much easier to increase spend than to recover it.
  • Check your currency. Spend is shown in the account currency — SGD in the example above.
  • Judge over weeks, not days. Early figures are noisy; give a campaign enough clicks to mean something before rewriting it.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Email designs
docs.text: The frame around your emails: the header with your logo, the footer with your address and unsubscribe link, and your colours and fonts. Make it once, and every email you write sits inside it.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Every email needs the same header, footer and legal lines. A design holds them, so you only write the message. Change the design once, for example a new logo, and the next emails use it.

docs.title: How to create a design
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Emails, then the Email Designs tab.
  2. Choose Create Design and start from a template, or Import your own HTML.
  3. Edit the header and footer. The middle part, shown as $content in the preview, is where each email's text goes.
  4. Save. The design appears in the list, ready to pick when you write an email.

docs.title: Where designs are used
docs.text:
• Emails: pick the design when you create an email. See Emails.
  • Events: pick one under the event's Definition → Email design; all its invitations, confirmations and reminders use it.
  • Forms: the confirmation email of a form uses the design you choose for it.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Keep the unsubscribe link. The footer's unsubscribe and privacy links are required for marketing emails; they are filled in for each recipient.
  • Use your Brand Kit. Colours and fonts from your Brand Kit keep every email on brand.
  • Editing a design does not change emails already sent.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Emails
docs.text: Design, send and track the emails you send to your contacts — from a one-off announcement to a regular newsletter.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Email is where most marketing plans still start. GoodBards keeps the whole job in one place: you pick a look, write the message, choose who receives it, and see how it performed — without exporting lists or switching to a separate email tool.

Because your emails sit alongside your contacts, anything you already know about your audience is available when you choose recipients.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• At least one contact in Audience → Contacts, or a mailing list to send to.
  • Your Brand Kit set up, if you want emails to pick up your colours and logo automatically. See Brand Kit.

docs.title: How to create an email
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Emails.
  2. Choose + Create Email.
  3. Pick how you want to start. GoodBards offers four options:
Option When to use it Designs Gallery The usual choice. Reuse a look and feel — header, footer and branding — and just write the message. Marked Recommended. Import from External You already have the email elsewhere. Paste HTML, upload a .eml file, upload a .zip export (for example from Canva), or fetch a URL. Reuse existing from platform Send something you have written before, with fresh recipients. Start Blank An empty email with no styling. Best for a plain, personal message.
  1. Work through the three steps at the top of the dialog: Look & Feel, then Content, then Recipients.
  2. Preview your email before sending, and send yourself a test if you can.

Reuse beats starting over

If you send a similar email regularly, Reuse existing from platform keeps the content and design and only asks for new recipients — usually faster than building it again.

docs.title: Importing a design from Canva
docs.text:
Canva exports an email as a .zip holding the email's HTML and its images.

  1. In Canva, export your email design. Keep the .zip as it is; there's no need to unzip it.
  2. In Create Email, choose Import from External, then the ZIP (Canva) tab, and drop the .zip. Any .zip with one HTML file and its images works the same way.
  3. Choose Analyze & clean up. The report lists what the file contained: the images found, any image the HTML uses but the .zip lacks, and files that won't be used.
  4. Check the Import name. It names the email and the folder its images go to.
  5. Continue through Scope and Images. The images are copied to Drive › My Documents › Images › your import name and made public so recipients can see them; the email points at those copies.

Good to know:

  • The plain-text version of the email is created from the HTML, with its links. The .txt file in Canva's export is not used.
  • Canva's unsubscribe link is converted automatically. If an email has no unsubscribe link, the report warns you: add one, or use a Design whose footer has it, before sending.
  • If the design uses a font recipients don't have (Canva's brand fonts, for example), the report names it and the font they'll see instead.
  • SVG images are not imported: Gmail and Outlook don't display them. Export them from Canva as PNG instead.

docs.title: Editing an email
docs.text:
Choose an email's preview in the gallery to open it. Its page shows the subject and the body as recipients will see it, with an Edit button on each, and Send Test Email.

Edit on the body opens the editor. The design (header and footer) is locked: you edit only your content inside it.

  • Visual: click any text to change it; drag blocks from the right (heading, text, button, image, two columns, divider…). Personal fields such as First name are filled in for each recipient; see Personalising an email.
  • Code: edit the HTML directly.
  • AI: describe the change, for example make it shorter and warmer. You can also paste links: write a newsletter from these posts followed by up to three web addresses builds a section per post, with a "Read more" link to each. The pages are read before the AI writes, and the panel tells you which ones it could read; a page whose owner blocks automated access is named, not guessed at.
  • Desktop, Email width and Mobile preview the email at each size.

Choose Apply to keep your changes, or Cancel.

The card menu in the gallery also offers Show Tactics (where the email is used), Duplicate, Attach to tactic and Delete.

docs.title: Personalising an email
docs.text:
A personal field is a placeholder between double curly braces, such as {{contact_firstname}}. When the email is sent, each recipient gets their own value in its place. Fields work in the subject as well as in the body.

  1. Open the email and choose Edit on the subject or the body.

  2. Type the field where the value should appear, braces included. In the Visual editor, type it into any text; in Code, anywhere in the HTML.

    Hi {{contact_firstname}}, here is what's new this month.

  3. Choose Apply, then Send Test Email to check it.

The fields you can use:

Field Filled with {{contact_firstname}} The recipient's first name {{contact_lastname}} The recipient's last name {{contact_email}} The recipient's email address {{contact_phone}} The recipient's phone number {{contact_job_title}} The recipient's job title {{company_name}} The company name, when the tactic sends one email per company {{unsubscribe_url}} The link to unsubscribe. Every design's footer already has it. {{privacy_policy_url}} The link to your privacy statement {{view_in_browser_url}} The link to open the email in a browser

Good to know:

  • A field the recipient has no value for is left blank. Hi {{contact_firstname}}, becomes Hi , for a contact without a first name. Keep names for lists you know are complete, or write the greeting so it reads well without one: Hello {{contact_firstname}} rather than Dear {{contact_firstname}},.
  • Test emails use your own contact record. The field is filled only when the address you send the test to exists in Audience → Contacts. Otherwise it shows blank in the test, and works for real recipients.
  • Spell fields exactly as above. {{first_name}} or {{FirstName}}, which other tools use, are not recognised and show as ??? in the sent email. If you import an email from Canva or another tool, replace its fields with the ones in the table.

docs.title: Attaching an email to a tactic
docs.text:
An email is sent from a campaign tactic: the tactic holds the audience, the sender and the send button. Attach to tactic in the card menu links the email to one, in three ways:

  • Existing tactic: pick a campaign, then one of its email tactics. Only tactics that can still take the email are listed: a tactic sends one email, so those that already sent theirs, and closed tactics, are left out. A tactic whose email is still a draft, failed, or scheduled is listed with that email's name; attaching replaces it after you confirm. The audience and the sender stay; a scheduled send is cancelled, and you schedule the new email again from the tactic page.
  • New tactic in a campaign: pick a campaign and name the tactic; it is created as a draft with the email attached.
  • New campaign: name the campaign, choose its objective and name the tactic; both are created with the email attached.

Each option opens the tactic page, where you set the recipients and send.

docs.title: Finding your emails
docs.text:
Everything you have created is listed under Email Gallery, on the Emails tab. Use the search box to find one by name, and the buttons beside it to switch between grid and list view.

The Email Designs tab holds the reusable looks — headers, footers and branding — rather than individual messages.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Emails and designs are separate. A design is the wrapper you reuse; an email is one message you send. Editing a design does not rewrite emails already sent.
  • Check the preview before every send. Email clients vary, and a layout that looks right in the editor can shift in Gmail or Outlook.
  • Sent emails cannot be recalled. Confirm your recipient list before the final step.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Event Management
docs.text: Run an event end to end: the registration page, the emails your guests receive, the waitlist, check-in on the day, and the follow-up afterwards.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Events usually mean juggling a registration page, a spreadsheet of attendees, a handful of emails and a clipboard at the door. Event Management keeps all of it on one page, and because every registration becomes a contact, following up afterwards does not mean re-typing a list.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• An email design for your brand, if you want the event emails to look like your other emails. Without one, they use the standard GoodBards design.
  • A form, if the default registration form (name, email, company, job title) is not enough.

docs.title: How to set up an event
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Event Management.
  2. Choose New Event and fill in the name, type, date, time and venue.
  3. Open the event. Its tabs follow the life of the event, left to right: Overview, Definition, Landing page, Registration, Communications, Attendance, Analytics, Follow-up.
  4. Work through them in that order. Everything saves on its own; there is no Save button on the event page.

docs.title: Definition: what guests see
docs.text: The Definition tab holds the cover image, the short and long descriptions, the date and the address. These feed the landing page and every event email: the event name, date and place in your emails always come from here. Change them here, never inside an email.

docs.title: Landing page
docs.text:
The Landing page tab shows the page guests register on. It is built from the Definition tab, so it is always up to date.

To change its layout, choose Duplicate to customize. You get your own copy in the visual editor.

A customized page is a copy

Once you customize the landing page, later changes on the Definition tab are no longer copied into it. Update the page yourself, or go back to the default.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
• Settings: capacity, the registration window, Require Approval, and the Waitlist.
  • Registration form: keep the default form, or choose Create new or Duplicate existing to use one of your own. Edit form opens it.
  • Contact registration: which form fields fill the contact record (email, first and last name, phone, job title, tags, custom fields). See Forms.
  • Registration emails: one email for each situation a guest can be in (see below).
  • Confirmation message: the text shown on the page after registering.

The last four blocks are folded; click a title to open it.

docs.title: Registration emails
docs.text:
Each email is sent automatically when a guest reaches that situation. Only the ones your event can produce are listed:

Email Sent when Listed when Confirmed The guest has a seat. Carries the check-in QR code and calendar links. Always Request received The guest registered and waits for your approval. Require Approval is on Approved You approved the request. Require Approval is on Declined You declined the request. You can turn this one off. Require Approval is on On the waitlist The event was full; the guest joined the waitlist. Waitlist is on Spot opened A seat freed up and the guest moved off the waitlist. Waitlist is on

docs.title: Editing an email
docs.text:
Every event email (the registration emails above, and the invitation and reminders under Communications) works the same way. The card shows the email as guests receive it, inside your event design.

  1. Click the preview, or Edit. The editor opens, with the Subject at the top and Visual, Code and AI on the side.
  2. Change the text, then choose Apply. The card now says Your own version of this email.
  3. To go back, choose Reset to standard.

In the Visual editor:

  • Purple dashed boxes are parts only some guests see. The title says who, for example Shown when the guest has a check-in QR code. Edit the text inside; the box itself cannot be moved or deleted, so the email keeps working for every guest.
  • Purple chips, such as Attendee name or Event location, are filled in for each guest when the email is sent. To add one, click into a text and pick it from Insert field… in the text toolbar. Do not type them by hand.

To send an email you built under Emails instead, choose Use one of my emails instead under the card.

docs.title: How to send, and see what happened
docs.text:
1. On Communications, choose Send Invitations to email your audience, or Send Reminder Now for a reminder.

  2. At the bottom of the tab, Sent emails lists every email the event has sent, with the time, the number of recipients and who sent it. Confirmations and other one-by-one emails are grouped per day.

  3. Choose Recipients on a line to see who received it, search them, or show the failed ones only. Choose Metrics for opens and clicks.

  4. On Attendance, the Latest email column shows the last email each guest received. The eye icon opens the guest's History with this event: what was sent, delivered, opened and clicked.

  5. On Analytics, Email Performance shows all the event's emails together or one type at a time, and Export CSV downloads the list.

docs.title: The waitlist
docs.text:
Turn on Waitlist under Registration › Settings. When the event is full, new registrations join a queue. Choose how a freed seat is given:

  • Automatic: the next person in line gets it and is emailed.
  • Manual: you choose. On Attendance, use ↑ Promote on a waiting guest. It only works when a seat is free.

docs.title: Checking people in
docs.text: On the day, use Scan attendee to check people in. Each guest's confirmation and reminder emails carry a QR code; scanning it records them as attended.

docs.title: The Actions menu
docs.text:
Action What it does Publish / Unpublish Puts the event page online, or takes it offline. Open public page Opens the event page as guests see it. Open / Close registration Starts or stops accepting registrations, without touching the event itself. Send invitations Emails the invitation to the event's audience. Scan attendee / Kiosk mode Checks guests in. See Check-in and badges. Export attendees Downloads the guest list as a spreadsheet. End event Ends it now; guests not checked in become absent. Ended events reopen with Reopen if you ended one too early. GoodBards also ends an event on its own when its end date passes. Cancel event Cancels it and emails every registered guest. Cannot be undone.

To run an event again, duplicate its tactic on the campaign page: the event comes with it. See Duplicating a tactic.

The Overview tab also has quick actions: Open Public Page, Copy Registration Link and Preview Invitation Email.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Publish before you share the link. A draft event does not accept registrations.
  • Declined guests can stay unaware. Turn off the Declined email and nobody you decline is emailed, even when you change a status by hand.
  • Cancel with ⊘, not with the status menu. Cancel registration (the ⊘ icon on a row) emails the guest and offers the seat to the waitlist. Changing the status from the menu only corrects the list.
  • Follow up while it is fresh. Attendees are contacts, so the Follow-up tab can email everyone who came, everyone who did not, or the people you invited who never registered.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text: Collect sign-ups, registrations and feedback, and have the responses flow into your audience automatically.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A form is how people tell you something: registering for an event, asking to be contacted, or rating an experience. Responses land in GoodBards rather than in a spreadsheet, so the people who reply become contacts you can market to.

Forms are also how you run satisfaction surveys (NPS, CSAT and similar) without a separate survey tool.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • A privacy statement, if you collect personal data: Brand & Context → General Information → Privacy Statements. Mark one as the company default and every form uses it unless you pick another.

docs.title: How to create a form
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Forms, then Create Form.

  2. Choose how to start:

    • Form Gallery (recommended): ready-made forms grouped by what they measure, such as Contact / demo request, Net Promoter Score (NPS), Event registration or Newsletter signup.
    • Reuse a form: a copy of one of your own forms.
    • Import: paste the HTML of a form you already have.
    • Start blank: an empty contact form.
    • Fill in Core definition: the Name, a Category and a Description.
    • Choose Edit form to change the fields (see below).
    • Choose Create. Set the form to Open when it should accept responses.

docs.title: Change the fields
docs.text:
Edit form opens the visual builder.

  • Add a field: drag it from Forms in the left panel: Text field, Email field, Phone field, Multi-line text, Dropdown, Checkbox, Consent.
  • Reorder: drag a field to its new place.
  • Make a field required: select it, open its settings (the gear icon on the right) and tick Required.
  • Choose Apply to keep your changes.

docs.title: Turn responses into contacts
docs.text:
In the Customer Data Platform block:

  1. Switch on Create CRM contact.
  2. Check the mapping table. Email must point to the field that holds the person's email address. First name and Last name are recommended.
  3. To fill more of the contact, choose Add Mapping and pick a contact field (Phone, Job title, Tags or one of your custom fields). Fill it from a Form field, or with a Fixed value (for example, tag everyone who replies with webinar-oct).
  4. Under Privacy statement, keep Company default or pick another statement.

docs.title: Use a form to register for an event
docs.text: Open the event, then Registration → Registration form. Pick your form, or choose Create new to start from the event registration template. The event then manages the form's confirmation email and thank-you page, under Registration → Confirmation. See Event Management.

docs.title: Sharing a form
docs.text:
From a form's menu in the list:

  • Copy Link copies the form's short link, to share in a post, a message or a QR code.
  • Embed form gives you a code to paste into your own website, so visitors fill in the form without leaving your site. Set the height you want; the form keeps its own design and adapts its height to the page.

docs.title: Categories and status
docs.text:
Category Use it for Registration & sign-ups Event registration, newsletter and webinar sign-ups. Experience metrics Satisfaction surveys: NPS, CSAT, CES, star ratings. Feedback & research Event and product feedback, general surveys. Data capture Contact and demo requests.

A form is a Draft while you build it and Open when it accepts responses.

docs.title: Reading the answers
docs.text:
In a form's menu, choose View Analytics to open its results: views and submissions over time, then every submission with its answers and date.

  • Download Raw CSV: every answer, one row per submission, for your own analysis.
  • Download Contact CSV: the people who answered, as contacts.

A view is one display of the form, whether people come from its link, an email button or your website. Your own clicks on Open Form and visits by robots are not counted.

Many views and few submissions usually means the form asks too much.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Consent is only recorded when the box is ticked. A form records a person's acceptance of your privacy statement only if it has a Consent field and they tick it. Without one, the editor warns you: drag the Consent block in.
  • A form must be Open to collect anything, even if you have shared the link.
  • Responses update existing contacts. A submission with an email address you already hold fills in that contact's empty fields; it never overwrites what is there.
  • Renaming a field is safe. The contact mapping follows the new name.
  • One form, one event. Picking a form already used by another event links a copy, so the two events never share answers.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Launch a Tactic
docs.text: Put out a single piece of marketing — one post, one email — without setting up a whole campaign first.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A tactic is one piece of marketing activity on one channel: a LinkedIn post, a TikTok video, an email newsletter. It is the smallest thing you can publish.

Most of the time you do not need a campaign. If you simply want something out on Instagram this afternoon, start here. Campaigns are for when several tactics work towards the same goal over a period of time — see Campaigns.

docs.title: How to launch a tactic
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Launch a Tactic.
  2. Pick the channel you want to publish on.

Channels are grouped by type, and each says what it is best suited to — LinkedIn for professional and B2B content, TikTok for short-form video, and so on. Once you have picked one, follow the steps for that channel to write your content and publish or schedule it.

Not sure which channel?

The short description under each one is a reminder of what that audience expects. Match the content to the channel rather than posting the same message everywhere.

docs.title: Available channels
docs.text:
Group Channels Social Media Twitter, Reddit, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Short YouTube Video, YouTube Video, Telegram, WhatsApp Emails Email Campaign — targeted newsletters and promotional emails

Use Search tactics… at the top right to jump straight to one.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• You need the channel connected first. A social channel you have not linked cannot publish. Set these up in Settings → Connections.
  • A tactic can be added to a campaign later. Starting with a single tactic does not lock you out of organising it into a campaign afterwards.
  • Each channel has its own rules on length, images and video. The tactic screen for that channel will tell you what it accepts.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Configure your account, your company, your brand and the services GoodBards connects to.

Who sees it: your own Personal Settings are open to everyone. Everything else needs the Settings access.

docs.title: Personal Settings
docs.text:
Your profile, password, language, default brand voice and your own AI memory.

See Personal Settings.

docs.title: Brand & Context
docs.text:
What the AI knows about your company: general information, privacy statements, your marketing campaign defaults, competitors and website.

See Brand & Context and How the AI knows your brand.

docs.title: Brand Kit
docs.text:
Logos, colours, fonts and tone of voice, used by every email, design and AI answer.

See Brand Kit.

docs.title: Voices Bank
docs.text:
Writing styles learned from real samples, such as your founder's posts.

See How the AI knows your brand.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
Link the outside services you use: social networks, Google Analytics and Search Console, Google Ads, your CRM.

See Connections.

docs.title: AI Settings
docs.text:
Which AI models your team uses, the tools and skills agents may use, and what the agents have learned.

See AI Settings.

docs.title: Users, roles & permissions
docs.text:
Invite colleagues and decide what each one can see and change. Access is given per module (Home, Audience, Marketing, Emails and forms, Events, Social media, Digital ads, Content hub, Website and SEO, AI studio, Tool box, Settings), each in read-only or read and write. Ready-made roles cover the usual cases: a Marketer sees everything, a Sales member sees the Audience and only the contacts they own.

See Users, roles & permissions.

docs.title: Sub-workspaces
docs.text:
Separate workspaces under your own, one per client, brand or business unit.

See Sub-Workspaces.

docs.title: Usage & Billing
docs.text:
What your team has used against your plan.

See Usage & Billing.

docs.title: Setting up for the first time
docs.text: In this order: Brand & Context, then Brand Kit, then Connections. The brand kit shapes everything the AI produces, so it is worth doing before generating content.

docs.title: AI Settings
docs.text: Choose which AI models your team uses, and what the AI is allowed to do.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
GoodBards can use different AI providers and models for different jobs. Most teams never need to change this — the defaults are sensible. It matters when you have a preference about which provider handles your content, or want a higher-quality model for one kind of work.

Changing a model here affects everyone in your company.

docs.title: How to change a default model
docs.text:
1. Open your account menu (your picture, top right), then choose AI Settings.
  2. On the Models tab, find the type of generation you want to change.
  3. Pick a Provider, then a Large Language Model (LLM) from that provider.

docs.title: The four generation types
docs.text:
Type Used for Text generation Writing — email copy, social posts, agent replies. Image generation Images created from a description. Video Generation Short video clips. Audio Generation Text to speech.

Each is set independently, so you can use one provider for writing and another for images.

Not every type needs to be set

A generation type showing Select Provider has no model configured. Those features will not work until you choose one.

docs.title: The other tabs
docs.text: Tab What it holds Models Default model per generation type, as above. MCP Tools External tools your agents may use. Skills Capabilities available to your agents. Learned Memory What the AI has remembered about your business over time. See How the AI knows your brand.

docs.title: MCP Tools: give your agents outside tools
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers let your AI agents use other services: read your Mailchimp or Klaviyo campaigns, post in Slack, manage a Wix or WordPress.com site, or reach thousands of apps through Zapier.

  1. On the MCP Tools tab, choose Connect on a service and sign in to it, or paste the key or URL it asks for (Zapier asks for your personal Zapier MCP URL).
  2. Once connected, its tools are available to your agents. Choose which agent uses them in the agent's settings.

Add Custom MCP Server connects any other MCP server by its address.

docs.title: Skills: ready-made expertise
docs.text: Skills are packaged know-how an agent can use, for example AI Search Optimization (GEO), Content Strategy Planner, Marketing Ideas, Marketing Plan Builder or Public Relations & Earned Media, each tuned for Southeast Asian markets. The tab lists the skills available to your company; you give a skill to an agent in the agent's configuration.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• These are company-wide defaults. Changing a model changes it for every colleague, not just you.
  • Models differ in cost as well as quality. A more capable model consumes credits faster — see Usage & Billing.
  • Test after changing. Generate a sample piece of content and check the tone still matches your brand before your team relies on it.
  • Leave it alone if unsure. The defaults are chosen to work well; this screen is for teams with a specific reason to change them.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Brand Kit
docs.text: Your colours, fonts and logos, in one place — so everything GoodBards produces looks like it came from you.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A brand kit is the visual half of your identity. Once set up, emails, social posts and generated images pick up your colours and logo without you specifying them each time.

It sits alongside the Voices Bank, which covers how your brand sounds. Together they are what makes AI output look and read like your brand rather than a generic template.

docs.title: How to set up your brand kit
docs.text:
1. Open your account menu (your picture, top right), then choose Brand & Context.
  2. Open the Brand Kit tab.
  3. Choose + Add Brand Kit.
  4. Add your colours, fonts and logo.
  5. Mark one kit as primary.

docs.title: Colour roles matter more than colour names
docs.text:
When you add a colour, you give it a role — what the colour is for, not what it is called. A colour named "Ocean Blue" means nothing to the platform; a colour assigned the role of primary or accent can be applied correctly everywhere.

If your generated designs use your colours in odd places, check the roles rather than the colours themselves.

docs.title: Applying your brand to the platform itself
docs.text:
Apply brand to app interface restyles GoodBards in your own colours and logo. Useful if your team should see their own branding rather than the GoodBards default.

This requires a primary brand kit. Until you mark one, the toggle explains that there is no primary kit yet.

docs.title: More than one kit
docs.text: You can hold several — useful for sub-brands or for an agency running different clients. The primary kit is the one used by default and the one that drives the interface.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Set this up early. Brand-aware content is only brand-aware from the moment the kit exists.
  • Use your real assets. Upload the actual logo files your designer produced, not screenshots of them.
  • Primary is the one that counts. With several kits, anything not explicitly told otherwise uses the primary.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: How the AI knows your brand
How the AI knows your brand
docs.text: Three things shape everything the AI writes for you: your Brand Context, the Brand Voice you pick, and what it has learned from working with you. This page explains what each one does and how to keep them right.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Without them, an agent writes generic copy and you re-explain your business in every request. With them, the same request comes back with your company's facts, in your style, following the rules you set.

What it is Who sets it When the AI uses it Brand Context Facts about your company: what you do, who you serve, how you are positioned, what never to say. Plus your primary Brand Kit (tone, keywords, hashtags). Your company admins, once. Every request, by every agent. Brand Voice A writing style learned from real samples, such as your founder's posts. Anyone builds voices; each person picks a default. Only when a voice is selected for the conversation. Memory Short facts learned from your conversations, or added by hand. Learned automatically, reviewed by you. In conversations with agents that have memory on.

Example. You ask: "Write a LinkedIn post announcing our webinar."

  • With nothing set up, you get a generic announcement.
  • With Brand Context, it names your product correctly, speaks to your target audience and never mentions pricing, because Guardrails says so.
  • With a Brand Voice selected, it sounds like your founder: short sentences, a question to open, no exclamation marks.
  • With Memory, it remembers you always add the registration link in the first comment, because you told it last week.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • To edit Brand Context, you need to be an administrator of your company account.

docs.title: How to set up your Brand Context
docs.text:
1. Go to Brand & Context → General Information.
  2. Choose Populate with AI and enter your Website URL: GoodBards reads your home page and a few key pages, and fills in the fields as drafts. This takes about a minute.
  3. Review each field. AI drafts are Hidden from AI until you choose Show to AI. A field you edit and Save becomes visible to AI.
  4. Fill in Guardrails → Never discuss with the topics the AI must avoid.
  5. On Marketing Campaigns, set your campaign defaults (audience, regions, objective).

See Brand & Context for every field.

docs.title: How to create a Brand Voice
docs.text:
1. Go to Brand & Context → Voices Bank and choose Create Voice.
  2. Give it a name, then add up to 10 samples of real writing: paste text with Add text sample, or choose documents with Add from Drive.
  3. The voice goes from Analyzing to Active in a few minutes. Open Details to read the profile it built: tone, structure, favourite phrases, do's and don'ts.
  4. To use it by default, go to Personal Settings → Preferences → Default brand voice. You can also pick a voice for one conversation from the Voice menu in the chat box.

docs.title: How to review what the AI has learned
docs.text:
• Company memory: AI Settings → Learned Memory. Facts shared by every agent and every user of your company. Each shows whether it was Learned from conversation or Added manually. Edit or delete any of them, or add one with Add To Memory.
  • Your own memory: Personal Settings → My Memory. Facts about you and how you work, seen only in your conversations. Turn Enable Personal Memory off to stop the AI using and collecting them.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Hidden fields never reach the AI. That includes every AI draft you have not reviewed yet. If the AI ignores something, check its badge first.
  • Changes take up to about ten minutes to reach the agents.
  • Only your primary Brand Kit is used. Its tone of voice, keywords and hashtags apply to every request; a Voices Bank voice applies only when selected.
  • A voice is applied when the conversation starts. Changing it halfway through has no effect; start a new conversation.
  • Company memory is shared with everyone in your company. Do not put personal or confidential details in it. Clear all memory cannot be undone.
  • Agents learn company facts only if allowed. An agent adds to company memory only when Promote Facts to Tenant is on in its settings (off by default). Learning starts after a conversation of several exchanges.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Brand & Context
docs.text: Everything GoodBards knows about your business — and what the AI is allowed to use when it writes for you.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
When an agent drafts an email or a social post, it needs to know who you are: what the company does, how it talks, who it competes with. This is where you tell it once, so you are not re-explaining your business in every prompt.

Get this right and everything the AI produces improves. Leave it empty and you get generic copy.

docs.title: The six tabs
docs.text: Tab What it holds General Information Company name, tagline, website and other basics. Brand Kit Colours, fonts and logos. See Brand Kit. Voices Bank How your brand sounds, so the AI writes in your voice. Marketing Campaigns Context about the campaigns you run. Competitors Who you compete with. Website Your website, as the AI reads it.

docs.title: How to fill in your company details
docs.text:
1. Open your account menu (your picture, top right), then choose Brand & Context.
  2. On General Information, fill in each field. Grey example text under each one shows the kind of answer expected.
  3. Changes save as you go.

Populate With AI fills the fields from your website; check what it wrote.

docs.title: The General Information blocks
docs.text: Block What to put Company Infos Company name, tagline, website, industry and addresses. Positioning What you do, your value proposition, target audience, mission, elevator pitch and differentiators. The AI reuses these in everything it writes, so be specific. Guardrails Never discuss: subjects the AI must stay away from, for example politics, religion or competitor bashing.
