  4. Tick the posts you want: Launch, Key figure, Question, In case you missed it. Each one shows when it is suggested to go out. Tick the channels.
  5. Check Link to the article. Add anything to emphasise under Anything to stress? (optional).
  6. Choose Write the brief, check it, then choose Generate.
  7. Click a post to review it, change its picture or plan it. You can close the window while the posts are written.

Nothing is published: every post waits on its channel as a draft for you to review.

docs.title: How to write a post yourself
docs.text: Choose New Post, pick the Asset Type, keep New Empty as the Creation Method, give it a Title and choose Create. Type the post, save it, then add it to a campaign and publish or schedule it. The full walkthrough, with screenshots, is in Create a social post from scratch.

docs.title: How to write a post with AI
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Social Media → Social Post, then New Post.
  2. Pick the Asset Type, for example a LinkedIn post.
  3. Under Creation Method, choose Write with AI, then Continue.

  4. Fill in What is it about?. Optionally tell the AI how to write it in Instructions for the AI: the angle, what to stress or leave out, the length or the hashtags (for example "Focus on the ROI for agencies, under 150 words, end with a question"). Then add Source and materials: the facts the post may use, typed in Notes & facts, web pages, or files from your Content Repository. Finish with Tuning (audience, tone, language, keywords).

    Instructions or notes?

    Instructions say how to write the post; the AI follows them. Notes & facts say what is true; the AI only uses them as facts to cite, and never takes orders from them.

    1. Choose Write the brief, check it, then Generate. The AI drafts the post, reviews it and revises it once.
    2. Read the score and the checks. Apply the suggestions you agree with, or use Ask for a change. Then choose Save as asset.

In the post editor, Improve With AI opens a small chat with the AI: ask for a change (more punchy, add three hashtags) and the post is rewritten within the channel's character limit, with Revert to undo. Paste a link (write a post about https://…) and the page is read first, so the post draws on what it actually says. AI Hashtags suggests hashtags once the post has ten words. The preview on the right shows the post as it will appear on the network, on desktop or mobile.

docs.title: Videos, documents, Reels and stories
docs.text:
A post can carry a video or a document instead of pictures. The file comes from your Content Repository: upload it there first, with + New → Video or Upload. Videos up to 2 GB are accepted, and a progress bar shows the upload.

A post holds one kind of media: pictures, one video, or one document. Adding one removes the other, and with a video or a document attached, no link preview card is shown.

docs.title: A video on LinkedIn
docs.text:
1. In the post editor, open Insert → Video… and pick the video.
  2. Check the title under it: LinkedIn prints it under the video. It starts as the file's name.
  3. The preview on the right plays the video.

LinkedIn takes MP4 files from 75 KB to 500 MB, between 3 seconds and 30 minutes long. Videos it does not take are greyed out in the list, with the reason.

docs.title: A document on LinkedIn
docs.text:
A PDF, PowerPoint or Word file is shown on LinkedIn as a document people swipe through, page by page. It is the way to post a carousel on a company page: put one slide per page in a PDF.

  1. In the post editor, open Insert → Document (PDF, PowerPoint, Word)… and pick the file.
  2. Check the title: LinkedIn prints it above the document.

LinkedIn takes files up to 100 MB and 300 pages.

docs.title: Instagram: Post or Reel
docs.text:
Instagram has two asset types. Choose the right one in New Post:

Asset type Holds Instagram Post (images) One picture, or a carousel of 2 to 10 pictures. Instagram Reel (video) One video, published as a Reel and also shown in your grid.

For a Reel, choose Pick the Reel video from the Drive (or Insert → Reel video…), then set the Cover frame at, in seconds: the moment of the video shown as its cover. The preview plays the video in the vertical 9:16 frame.

Instagram takes Reels in MP4 or MOV, up to 300 MB, between 3 seconds and 15 minutes. Vertical 9:16 videos look best.

docs.title: Publish to Instagram as a story
docs.text:
Any Instagram post or Reel can go out as a story instead: in the Publish or Schedule window, set Publish as to Story.

  • A story shows for 24 hours. It shows the main picture, or the video, without the caption.
  • A video story must be under 100 MB, and 60 seconds at most.
  • Its numbers (views, reach, replies) are collected every 2 hours while it is live, and appear on the Stories card of your Instagram report. See Social Media Analysis.

docs.title: How to publish or schedule a post
docs.text:
Social Media → Social Post lists your posts as cards. The band on top shows whether a post is Scheduled or Published, and on which date.

  1. On Social Post, choose View Tactics on the post's card, then Add to Tactic. Choose the campaign and a compatible tactic, then Add to Tactic. (Or, from the campaign's social tactic, choose Import Asset and pick the post.)
  2. In the tactic, open the post's ⋮ menu:
    • Publish: choose the Destination and confirm.
    • Schedule: choose a Date & Time, or use AI Recommendations for the best slot, then Confirm Schedule.
  3. The card shows Scheduled or Published with the date.

A post with a video or a document takes longer: the file is sent to the network, which then processes it. The post shows Sending in the tactic, then Published, usually within a few minutes. You can leave the page meanwhile. If the network refuses the file, the post shows Error: hover it to read the network's reason, fix the file, and publish again.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Character limits are per channel: 3,000 on LinkedIn, 280 on X, 2,200 on Instagram and TikTok. The text box turns red past the limit.
  • Media or link preview, not both. With a picture, a video or a document attached, LinkedIn and Facebook do not show the link's preview card. Without one, the preview card shows, but Instagram still needs a picture or a video.
  • Videos and documents are for LinkedIn and Instagram. Documents are for LinkedIn only. Instagram carousels hold pictures only, not videos.
  • Published posts are locked. You cannot edit or delete them from GoodBards.
  • Posted outside GoodBards? In the tactic, choose Link published post and paste its link: its results then count in the campaign report.
  • LinkedIn personal profiles do not give analytics; publish to a company page if you want results.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Tool Box
docs.text:
Small standalone utilities for the everyday jobs around a marketing plan.

Who sees it: everyone your administrator gives the Tool box access to.

docs.title: Web Scraping
docs.text:
Pull the content of a web page so GoodBards can work with it, for example to brief the AI on a competitor's page.

See Web Scraping.

docs.title: External Chatbot
docs.text:
A chatbot on your own website that answers visitors' questions and captures leads as contacts.

See External Chatbot.

docs.title: QR Code Gen
docs.text:
Branded QR codes for print, packaging and events.

See QR Code Generator.

docs.title: URL Shortener
docs.text:
Short, trackable links.

See URL Shortener.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
Run an AI agent or a report on a schedule, every morning or every Monday, and receive the result by email or in your Content Repository.

See Scheduler.

docs.title: Image Editor
docs.text:
Crop, resize and adjust images without leaving GoodBards.

See Image Editor.

These tools work on their own. None needs a campaign before you can use it.

docs.title: External Chatbot
docs.text: Put a GoodBards agent on your own website, to answer visitors' questions around the clock.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Visitors ask the same questions at all hours — opening times, pricing, whether you serve their industry. The external chatbot puts one of your chat agents on your website to answer them, styled to match your brand.

Because it is one of your agents, it knows your business rather than reciting a scripted FAQ.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A chat agent to put on the site. See Chat Agents.
  • Someone who can add a snippet of code to your website.

docs.title: How to configure the chatbot
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → External Chatbot.
  2. On the Settings tab, choose which Agent answers visitors.
  3. Write the Welcome message shown when the chat opens.
  4. Set the branding — icon, title, colours and sizes.
  5. Watch the Preview on the right update as you go.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
Setting What it controls Agent Which of your agents answers. Welcome message The greeting when someone opens the chat. Language The interface language of the widget. Theme Light or dark. Change Icon Your logo on the chat bubble. Square, up to 1 MB. Title Label The name at the top of the window. Font Size / Icon Size How large the widget appears. User / System Message Colours Colours for visitor and bot messages. Bubble Message The prompt on the closed bubble — for example Hi there! Need help?

The preview is live

The panel on the right shows exactly what visitors will see. Check it in both light and dark themes before publishing — colour choices that work in one can be unreadable in the other.

docs.title: Putting it on your website
docs.text: The Embed tab gives you the code to add to your site. Send it to whoever maintains your website, or paste it in yourself if you manage the site.

docs.title: Seeing how it performs
docs.text: Dashboard Analytics shows what visitors have been asking. Worth reviewing regularly — recurring questions usually mean something is unclear on your website, and the answer is often to fix the page rather than the bot.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Test it before launch. Ask the questions your customers actually ask and check the answers are right.
  • Your agent's knowledge is the bot's knowledge. If it cannot answer, improve the agent or your Brand & Context rather than the widget.
  • Say it is a bot. Visitors dislike discovering late that they were not talking to a person.
  • Keep a route to a human. Some questions need one — make sure the bot does not become a dead end.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Image Editor
docs.text: Crop, resize and adjust images without leaving the platform.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Marketing images rarely arrive the right size. A photo needs cropping for a banner, a logo needs resizing for an email header, a picture needs brightening before it goes out.

Small jobs like these do not warrant design software, and the editor handles them in place — so you are not exporting files back and forth.

docs.title: How to edit an image
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → Image Editor.
  2. Load your image one of three ways:
  3. Drop it on the upload area, or choose it to browse.
  4. Paste URL to pull an image from the web.
  5. Load From Drive to use a file you already hold in Drive.
  6. Use the editing tools — crop, resize, filters and adjustments.
  7. Save the result.

docs.title: The editing tabs
docs.text:
Once an image is loaded, the panel on the right has four tabs:

Tab What you can do Style Filters, and adjustments such as brightness, contrast and saturation. Transform Crop, rotate and zoom. Resize Resize to a preset for each social network, or to your own size. AI Describe the change in words, for example remove the background or add a sunset sky, and the AI edits the image. With no image loaded, it generates one from your description.

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
JPG, PNG, WebP and GIF.

Load from Drive to keep things tidy

If the image is already in Drive, use Load From Drive rather than downloading and re-uploading it. Fewer copies means less confusion later about which version is current.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Crop for the destination. An email header, an Instagram post and a website banner all want different shapes. Crop a copy for each rather than compromising with one.
  • Resize down, not up. Making a small image larger makes it blurry; the detail is not there to recover.
  • Keep the original. Save edits as a new file so you can go back if a later campaign needs a different crop.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: QR Code Generator
docs.text: Create QR codes for print, packaging and events — styled to match your brand.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: A QR code turns a printed thing into a link: a poster into a sign-up page, a business card into your website, a table tent into a feedback form. This tool makes them without a third-party site, and can track how often each one is scanned.

docs.title: How to generate a QR code
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → QR Code Gen.
  2. Enter the destination in URL. The preview appears once the URL is valid.
  3. Style it to match your brand using the options below.
  4. Download the finished code.

docs.title: Styling options
docs.text:
Option Choices QR Style Squares, Dots, Fluid — how the code's dots are drawn. Color A set of preset colours, or the picker for your own. Marker Border Square, Rounded, Circle — the outer shape of the three corner markers. Marker Center Square, Circle — the inner shape of those markers. Center Logo Upload Logo places your logo in the middle.

Test before you print

Heavy styling can make a code harder to scan — pale colours, a large centre logo, or the Fluid style on a small print size. Always scan the finished code with a real phone before sending anything to print.

docs.title: Tracking scans
docs.text:
Track URL beside the URL field turns the code into a tracked link, so you can see how many people scanned it. This uses the URL Shortener behind the scenes.

Worth doing whenever the QR code goes somewhere you cannot otherwise measure — a printed flyer, a conference banner, product packaging.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The code points at a URL, not a file. If the destination page moves, the printed code breaks. Use a tracked link so you can repoint it later.
  • Contrast matters. Dark code on a light background scans most reliably.
  • Size for the distance. A code on a poster read from across a room needs to be far larger than one on a business card.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text: Run recurring work on a schedule: an AI agent's report every Monday, a social report every month, a web page checked every morning.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Some work is the same every week: summarise last week's results, check a competitor's page, collect the social figures for a client. The Scheduler does it for you at the time you choose, and sends you the result by email or saves it in your Content Repository.

docs.title: How to schedule a task
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → Scheduler, then New Task.

  2. Give the task a Name and, if you like, a Description, then pick the Task type:

    Task type What it does Agent run Asks one of your AI agents a question, for example "Summarise last week's campaign results". Social report Builds the period report of one of your social accounts. Web scrape Reads a web page, for example a competitor's pricing page. Drive sync Brings files from a connected storage into your Content Repository.

  3. Choose Next, then fill in the Details: which agent and what to ask, which social account, which page. For an agent run, choose where the answer goes: an email to you or your colleagues, a document in your Content Repository, or both.

  4. Choose Next, then set the Schedule: how often and at what time.
  5. Save. The task appears in the list with its next run; open it to see the history of its runs.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A task runs as the person who created it, with that person's access. An administrator can choose to run it as another member.
  • If the delivery fails, the run still counts. For example, the agent answers but the email cannot be sent: the history shows the run in amber with the reason.
  • A scheduled agent does not act on its own. When it runs unattended, it will not send a campaign email or publish content; it can prepare them for you.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Translator
docs.text: Translate marketing copy between the languages your markets speak, keeping the formatting intact.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Southeast Asia is not one audience. The same campaign may need English in Singapore, Bahasa in Indonesia and Chinese in Taiwan — and a translation that reads naturally in each.

The Translator works on formatted text, so headings, bold, lists and links survive. You can paste copy in or import a file.

docs.title: How to translate content
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Content Hub → Translator.
  2. Put your copy into Source Text — type it, paste it, or use Import File.
  3. Set Source Language and Source Region.
  4. Set Target Language and Destination Region.
  5. Choose TRANSLATE.

Next to the translation, AI Translation Insights explains the Context the AI took into account and gives Quality Notes: places where a term was adapted rather than translated word for word, or where you may want a native speaker to check.

docs.title: Why region matters as well as language
docs.text:
The tool asks for a region alongside each language, and the pairing changes the result. Chinese for Singapore is not Chinese for Taiwan; English for Malaysia carries different conventions from English for the United States.

Setting both means you get copy that reads as though it were written locally, rather than a literal translation.

Formatting is preserved

Because the source box is a full editor, bold, headings, lists and links come through the translation. Format your copy before translating rather than reformatting afterwards.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Have a native speaker check anything important. AI translation is strong on fluency but can miss tone, idiom and cultural nuance — exactly the things that matter in marketing copy.
  • Translate the finished copy. Translating a draft you go on to edit means doing the work twice.
  • Watch length. Translated text often runs longer or shorter than the original, which can break a layout — check email and ad designs after translating.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: URL Shortener
docs.text: Turn long links into short ones, and see how often each is clicked.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Two reasons to shorten a link. It looks tidier in a social post, an SMS or on print. More usefully, a shortened link is a tracked link — you can see how many people clicked, which tells you whether a channel is working.

docs.title: How to shorten a link
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → URL Shortener.
  2. Choose + New Link.
  3. Paste the destination URL and save.
  4. Copy the short link and use it wherever you need.

Before you create your first link, the list is empty — as above. Every link you create appears here with its click count.

docs.title: Finding a link later
docs.text: Use Search links… to find one by name or destination, and View to change which columns are shown.

docs.title: A link's menu
docs.text:
The menu at the end of each row offers:

  • QR code: a QR code for the short link, to print on a flyer or in a store.
  • Click timeline: the link's clicks day by day.
  • Edit: change the title, the destination or the UTM tags. The short code stays the same, so links already shared keep working.
  • Delete.

docs.title: Where shortened links are used
docs.text:
Beyond links you create by hand, the shortener is used elsewhere in the platform:

  • The QR Code Generator uses it when you enable Track URL.
  • Links in emails can be tracked the same way, which is what click reporting is built on.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Shortened links are permanent-ish. Once printed or posted, you cannot take them back — so do not delete a link that is still in circulation.
  • Name links so you recognise them. Q4 flyer — Orchard Road beats a row of identical-looking codes.
  • One link per placement. Using a separate link for the flyer and the poster tells you which one worked. Reusing one link for both tells you nothing.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Organic Visibility
docs.text:
How your website is found, in search engines and in AI assistants, and what to fix first.

Who sees it: everyone your administrator gives the Website and SEO access to.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: These screens read your Google Search Console and Google Analytics data. If a screen says you are not connected, start at Connections.

docs.title: Performance & Report
docs.text:
How your site performs in search over time: clicks, impressions and position, with the trend and what to expect next. Other tabs give an executive report to share and a health check of your site.

See Performance & Report.

docs.title: Page Fixes
docs.text:
The pages worth fixing first: pages close to the top of the results, pages losing traffic, and pages people see but rarely click. Each card says what to change, and you can send it to Actions.

See Page Fixes.

docs.title: AI Readiness & Authority
docs.text:
Whether AI assistants can read, trust and quote your pages, scored page by page, and how often they mention you when asked about your market.

See AI Readiness & Authority.

docs.title: Momentum
docs.text:
The pages that are rising or falling right now, so you can act while it matters. In the sidebar it sits under Content Hub.

See Momentum.

docs.title: Google Analytics
docs.text:
Traffic and visitor behaviour on your site.

See Google Analytics.

docs.title: Google Trends
docs.text:
What your market is searching for, and how interest changes over time.

See Google Trends.

docs.title: AI Readiness & Authority
docs.text: Whether AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity can read, trust and quote your pages, and how often they mention you.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: More and more people ask an AI assistant instead of searching. The assistant quotes pages that answer clearly, show who wrote them, use structured data and stay up to date. This screen scores your pages on those points and tells you what to fix first.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Organic Visibility → AI Readiness & Authority.
  2. The Page Readiness tab gives the overall score out of 100 and one score per pillar.
Pillar What it checks Answers & FAQ Questions answered plainly on the page. Structured data Schema markup that tells machines what the page is. Content structure Clear headings, lists and short sections. Content trust signals Author, sources, dates, contact details. Quotability Sentences an assistant can quote as they are. Freshness How recently the page was updated.
  1. Under Recommendations, work through the items in order; each one can go to the Action Queue.

Scan More Pages adds pages to the scan; Rescan Pages updates the scores after you changed them.

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text: Tab What it shows Page Readiness The scores above. AI Mentions Whether AI assistants mention your brand. Structured Data The schema markup on your pages. Site Tools Site-wide checks and tools for AI crawlers. Authority Who finds you by name and who finds you without knowing you, and the trust signals (experience, expertise, authority) you assess yourself.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A pillar that does not apply is left out, not counted as zero. A contact page is not expected to have an FAQ.
  • Start with Answers & FAQ. It is usually the lowest score and the fastest to raise: add the questions your customers really ask, with short answers.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Google Analytics
docs.text: See how many people visit your website, where they come from, and what they do when they arrive.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Your website is usually where marketing ends up — the click from an email, the link in a social post, the QR code on a flyer. Google Analytics tells you whether any of it worked.

Bringing it into GoodBards means you can read your traffic beside your campaigns, rather than switching to a separate tool.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need Google Analytics connected, and a GA4 property chosen. If this page tells you that you are not connected, start at Connections.

docs.title: How to read your traffic report
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Organic Visibility → Google Analytics.
  2. Check the GA4 Property shown — this is the website being reported on.
  3. Pick a Time Period, such as Last 7 days.

Give it a moment

This page pulls live data from Google and can take several seconds to fill in. Empty charts usually mean it is still loading, not that there is no data.

docs.title: The four headline numbers
docs.text: Metric What it means What to watch for Total Visits Every visit, including repeat visits by the same person. Sudden drops usually mean a technical problem. Unique Visitors How many different people visited. The gap between this and total visits shows how often people return. Avg. Session Duration How long a visit lasts. Very short sessions suggest visitors are not finding what they expected. Bounce Rate The share who left without going any further. High bounce on a campaign landing page means the page is not matching the promise that brought them there.

docs.title: The charts
docs.text:
Website Visits by Day plots visits and unique visitors over time. Use it to check whether a campaign moved the numbers — look for the lift on the days you published.

Traffic Sources breaks visits down by where they came from: search, social, direct, referral. This is the chart that tells you which channel is actually delivering.

docs.title: The other tabs
docs.text:
Tab What it shows Traffic Visits, visitors and sources, as above. Revenue Overview Revenue attributed to your website. Intent Analytics What visitors appear to be looking for. Journey Mapper The paths visitors take through your site. Friction Finder Where visitors get stuck or drop out. ROI Tracker Return on your marketing spend.

Friction Finder and Journey Mapper are the two worth returning to. Traffic tells you how many arrived; these tell you why they left.

docs.title: Friction Finder
docs.text: A four-step funnel from arriving through search to buying, and the step where most people are lost, with the page responsible.

docs.title: Journey Mapper
docs.text:
Where people arriving from search land (left) and what they do next (right). Hover a band to highlight one path.

On these analysis tabs, Fetch from GA4 loads the latest figures for the date range; the date of the last fetch is shown under it. Generate Insights asks the AI Marketing Advisor what to do about what it sees.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Check the property. If the figures look wrong, confirm the GA4 Property is the site you meant — an account can hold several.
  • Compare like with like. Traffic has weekly rhythms, so compare a week with a week rather than a weekend with a Tuesday.
  • Analytics data lags slightly. Today's numbers may still be settling; judge campaigns after a few days.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Google Trends
docs.text: See what your market is searching for, when interest peaks, and how two ideas compare.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Before committing to a campaign it helps to know whether anyone is looking for what you are about to promote. Google Trends shows search interest over time, so you can spot a rising topic, catch a seasonal peak while it is still climbing, or settle an argument about which of two product names people actually search for.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Google Trends must be connected. If the page says you are not connected, go to Connections.

docs.title: How to compare search interest
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Organic Visibility → Google Trends.
  2. Type a term into Add a search term and press Enter.
  3. Add a second term to compare against the first.
  4. Set Location and Time Period.

Each term gets its own colour, matching its line on the chart. Remove one with the × on its card.

docs.title: Reading the chart
docs.text:
Interest over time plots each term across the period. Hover any point to see the figures for that day.

One term and two terms are measured differently

With a single term, the numbers are relative — 100 is that term's own peak for the period, not an absolute count. Add a second term and the chart shows estimated search volume instead, which is what makes comparison meaningful.

The shape matters more than the numbers. A line climbing steadily is a topic worth being early on; a sharp spike that falls away is a moment that has passed.

docs.title: Breakdown by location
docs.text:
Below the chart, Breakdown by location shows where your terms were most popular, sorted by whichever term you choose.

No sub-region data for Singapore

Google does not provide a sub-region breakdown for every location. For Singapore it returns nothing — the section tells you to pick another location or Worldwide. This is a limitation of Google's data, not a fault in GoodBards.

docs.title: Choosing a location
docs.text: Location sets the market you are looking at, and it changes the answer completely. A term that is rising in Singapore may be flat in Indonesia. If you market across Southeast Asia, check each market separately rather than assuming one stands for the others.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Compare like with like. Two terms on one chart is more useful than one term in isolation, because it gives you a sense of scale.
  • Interest is not intent. People searching a term are not necessarily ready to buy — pair this with your own analytics.
  • Watch for seasonality. Widen the time period before concluding a rise is new; it may be the same peak that happens every year.
  • Recent days may be incomplete. Google's most recent figures are still settling, so treat the last point on the chart with caution.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Momentum
docs.text: Your pages that are gaining or losing ground right now, so you can act while the trend is on your side.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: A page that suddenly gets more attention is worth a push now, not next quarter: a link from your newsletter, a social post, an update. A page that is losing ground needs a look before it disappears. Momentum ranks your pages by how fast they are moving.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • Google Search Console and Google Analytics connected under Connections.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Content Hub → Momentum.
  2. Filter by stage: Rising, Peaking, Plateau or Declining.

Each card shows the page, its momentum score out of 100 with the change, the trend line, and its clicks, position and impressions. Open a card for the search queries behind it and the visitors' engagement.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Momentum counts all visits, from search, social, email and other sites, not only Google search.
  • The advice at the top depends on your site type, detected automatically; choose Edit to correct it.
  • For pages that rank but under-perform, use Page Fixes instead.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Page Fixes
docs.text: The pages worth fixing first, ranked by the clicks the fix could bring, each with what to change.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Most sites have a few pages that already rank but lose the click, or that are close to the first page. Fixing those is the quickest search win there is. Page Fixes finds them in your Search Console data and puts the biggest ones first.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • Google Search Console connected under Connections.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Organic Visibility → Page Fixes.

  2. Pick a filter at the top:

    Filter The pages it shows Quick Wins Pages just below the top results, where a small push moves them up. Declining Pages losing traffic. Low CTR Pages people see but rarely click.

  3. Read the first card: the page, why it is listed, its impressions, click rate and position, and the expected impact.

  4. Open How to fix for the steps, then choose Add To Queue to put the work in Actions, or Not Now to set it aside.

docs.title: Three ways to look
docs.text:
The three icons at the top right switch the view:

  • List: the cards above, ranked by expected impact.

  • Chart: every page with an open finding, by position (further right is better) and click rate. Bubble size is how often the page was seen, colour is its main issue. Pages well below the dashed line are seen but not clicked. Click a bubble to open its card.

  • Competing pages: searches where several of your own pages compete for the same query, so neither ranks as well as one would. Searches on your brand name are marked Your brand: competing there is normal.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The ranking is tuned to your business. The line at the top right, such as SaaS / Software product, shows the site type used to judge what is normal.
  • Low CTR fixes are cheap. A better title and description take minutes and need no new content.
  • Check the result after a few weeks. Search Console needs time to show the effect; Performance & Report → Impact shows it.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Performance & Report
docs.text: How your site does in Google search: clicks, impressions, position and click rate, the trend, and a one-page report to share.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Search traffic moves slowly and in waves, so a single day says little. This screen shows the period against the one before, the trend line with a short forecast, and the patterns worth knowing about, such as a week below average.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Google Search Console connected under Connections, for your website.
  • For the business results (conversions, sessions), Google Analytics too.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Organic Visibility → Performance & Report.
  2. Pick the period at the top right, for example Last 28 days.
Figure What it means Clicks Visits from Google search results. Impressions How often your pages appeared in results. Avg. position Where you appear on average; lower is better (1 is the top). CTR Clicks divided by impressions.

Under the trend, Patterns detected points out runs of days above or below average.

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text:
Tab What it shows Overview The figures above and the trend. Executive Report A one-page read for someone who does not want the detail, with business outcomes from Google Analytics and a written summary. Impact What your work actually changed. Only items with a measured before and after count as verified. Signals Patterns in your figures that are unlikely to be chance. Most weeks have none, and that is a result too. Site Health & Settings Your site's type and language, which tune what the screens show and the advice they give. Diagnostics Which site and analytics property the screens read, and whether each Google connection works. Check it when a screen looks empty.

Write It Again rewrites the summary for your manager from the latest numbers.

docs.title: Impact: did the work pay off?
docs.text: Every fix you complete from Actions is measured: the page's figures before the change against after. Verified wins are fixes with a measured improvement; Awaiting measurement are fixes too recent to judge yet.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Position going down is good news. A drop from 17.5 to 13.7 means you moved up the results.
  • Impressions up, clicks flat usually means you rank for more searches but the titles do not make people click. See Page Fixes.
  • Search Console data is two to three days behind. The last days of the period are not complete yet.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Web Scraping
docs.text: Pull the content of a web page into GoodBards so you can work with it.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Sometimes the information you need is on a page rather than in a file — a competitor's pricing, a partner's announcement, an article you want summarised. Scraping extracts the text so an agent can read it or you can store it.

Three ways to gather content, on the tabs across the top:

Tab What it does Scrape One page, once. Crawl Follows links to gather several pages. Feed Scan Watches an RSS feed for new items.

docs.title: How to scrape a page
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Tool Box → Web Scraping.
  2. On the Scrape tab, paste the address into URL.
  3. Adjust the options if you need to.
  4. Run the scrape. The text appears under Result.

docs.title: The options
docs.text:
Option What it does When to change it Timeout (ms) How long to wait before giving up. Defaults to 30,000 (30 seconds). Raise it for slow sites. Save to Drive Stores the result as a file. When you want to keep it rather than read it once. Include links Captures outbound links as well as text. On by default; useful for finding related pages. Include HTML Returns the full markup, not just the text. Rarely needed — the text is usually what you want. Wait for network idle Waits for the page to finish loading. On by default. More complete, but slower. Force refresh Fetches again rather than reusing a cached copy. When checking a page you know has just changed.

Leave the defaults alone to start

The default settings work for most pages. If a scrape comes back empty or incomplete, raise the timeout first — slow-loading pages are the usual cause.

docs.title: Crawling a whole site
docs.text: On the Crawl tab, give a Start URL: GoodBards follows the links from that page, up to a Max depth (how many clicks away) and Max pages. Keep Same domain only on to stay on that website. Choose Start Crawl; a crawl runs in the background and can take several minutes. Crawl jobs lists your crawls, newest first; expand a finished one to see its pages.

docs.title: Following a news feed
docs.text: On the Feed Scan tab, give an RSS or Atom feed (or a page that has one) and how many entries to read, then Start Feed Scan. With Save to Drive on, each entry is saved in your Content Repository, so your agents can use it. Use it to follow an industry blog or a competitor's news.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Some sites cannot be scraped. Pages behind a login, or ones that block automated access, will not return content.
  • Scrape responsibly. Check the site's terms before pulling content repeatedly, and do not republish what you collect as your own.
  • Content is a snapshot. A scrape captures the page as it was at that moment; re-run it if you need current information.
  • Text, not layout. Extraction gives you the words. Design, images and formatting are not preserved.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: Your to-do list: what is worth doing next, ranked, with the evidence behind each item.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text: Reports tell you what happened; Actions tells you what to do about it. Each daily check (your website, social channels, emails and events) turns what it finds into an action, ranked by impact and effort. Your team adds its own asks to the same list, so everything worth doing is in one place, and every action is measured once it is done.

docs.title: How to work through your actions
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Actions. It opens on Priority: what to do first.
  2. Where to focus groups the open actions by impact and effort. Start with the Quick wins (high impact, low effort), then the Big bets.
  3. Below, the list is ranked by impact, confidence and effort. Narrow it with All sources, Mine (assigned to you) or the search box.

  1. Click an action to open it: what was found, the evidence, and where it stands.

  2. Choose Take Over to start it, assign it to a colleague, Mark As Done when finished, or Dismiss it if it does not apply. Use the arrows at the top to move to the next action.

To add your own, choose Add An Ask.

docs.title: How an action moves
docs.text: Stage Meaning To do Found, not started yet. Doing Someone is on it. Done Finished. GoodBards then measures the effect. Checking The effect is being measured. Verified The change worked. Dismissed Not relevant to you; set aside.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Your own asks come first in the ranking, ahead of the automatic ones.
  • An empty list is good news. The checks have run and found nothing needing attention. New actions appear as they run.
  • Actions depend on your connections. With nothing connected, there is little for the checks to read. See Connections.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text: Everything you have planned, across every channel, on one timeline.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Marketing goes wrong in the gaps: two emails on the same morning, a campaign that quietly has nothing scheduled for three weeks, a launch post that clashes with a public holiday. The calendar shows all of it together so you can see those problems before your audience does.

Anything scheduled — social posts, emails, events, campaign tactics — appears here automatically. You do not maintain it separately.

docs.title: How to read your calendar
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Marketing → Calendar, or the Calendar icon in the top bar.
  2. Switch between Week, Month and Year depending on how far ahead you are looking.
  3. Use the arrows beside the date range to move through time.

The header tells you what is in view — for example August 2026, 5 events.

docs.title: The campaigns panel
docs.text:
Down the left is every campaign overlapping the period you are viewing, each with its status, objective, date range and how many tactics it contains.

Each campaign has a coloured dot, and that colour is how its items appear in the grid — so you can see at a glance which campaign is driving a busy week.

Showing 5 out of 6 campaigns

The panel says how many campaigns it is displaying. If that number is lower than your total, some are filtered out — check Filter before concluding something is missing.

docs.title: Days with more than fits
docs.text: A day with several items shows the first few and then + 3 more. Choose that to see everything scheduled for the day.

docs.title: Opening an item
docs.text: Choose any item to see it in a side panel: its status, network, date and time, objective and campaign, and the content itself.

docs.title: Adding to the calendar
docs.text:
Most things arrive here on their own: schedule an email, a social post or an event and it appears without further work.

Create Event adds your own entry. Choose its type:

  • Event: something to remember, such as a trade show or a sale weekend.
  • Blackout: a period when nothing should go out, such as a public holiday or a crisis. It shows on the calendar so the team does not schedule into it.

Give it a title, a colour, the start and end (or All day), and a description.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The calendar reflects, it does not control. Move a post by editing the post, not by dragging it here.
  • Look for gaps as well as clashes. A month with nothing in it is as much a problem as a day with six things.
  • Check before you schedule. A quick look at the week you are aiming for avoids stacking three emails on the same morning.

Still stuck? Contact support.

docs.title: Content Repository
docs.text: Where the images, documents and files your marketing uses are stored. It used to be called Drive.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
Marketing runs on files — logos, product photography, brochures, the PDF you attach to a follow-up email. Drive keeps them in one place, so anything you use in a campaign, email or social post is already to hand rather than sitting on someone's laptop.

Files here are available to your whole team, and to the AI features that need them.

docs.title: How to upload and organise files
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, choose Content Hub → Content Repository, or the repository icon in the top bar.
  2. Open a folder to work inside it.

  3. Choose + New:

    Option What it does Upload Adds a file from your computer. Give it a marketing stage and, if it should not be used after a date, an expiration date. Add Website Adds a web page by its address; GoodBards reads its content so the AI can use it. Import WordPress Brings in your existing WordPress articles. Connect WordPress first under Connections. Folder Creates a folder.

Each file's Actions menu lets you share, move, rename or delete it, and see where it is used, for example in which campaigns and tactics.

docs.title: Editing an article or a post
docs.text:
Open an article or a post to edit it in the Asset Studio.

  • Improve With AI (or Cmd+J) opens a small chat with the AI editor. Ask for a change, for example shorter and warmer, and the whole document is rewritten; the change applies straight away, and Revert undoes it. Paste links in your request (draft this from https://…) and the pages are read before the AI writes; the chat says which ones it could read.
  • Quality Review scores the piece, as in the Content Workspace, and says what to improve.
  • Preview shows it as it will be published; Autosave saves as you type.
  • The ⋯ menu offers Create social posts (a series of posts from an article), exports to HTML, Markdown or JSON, Duplicate and Delete.

docs.title: The default folders
docs.text:
A new account starts with three:

Folder What it holds My Documents Your team's content, in Assets (articles and posts), Emails, Images, Audios and Videos, plus anything you upload. Shared With Me What colleagues have shared with you. System Files GoodBards manages itself. Leave this alone.

Do not reorganise System

The System folder holds files the platform depends on. Moving or deleting things here can break emails and campaigns that reference them.

docs.title: Finding files
docs.text:
• Search by title… finds a file by name. Switch from Title to Content to search inside documents instead.
  • The AI switch on a file lets the AI agents read it as background, for example your brand guidelines.
  • Filter narrows by file type and other attributes.
  • The two buttons beside Filter switch between list and grid view. Grid shows thumbnails, which is quicker for images.
  • The refresh button reloads the folder if you have just uploaded something elsewhere.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Name files so others can find them. logo-primary-dark.png is findable; Screenshot 2026-08-14 at 15.22.11.png is not.
  • Upload once, use everywhere. A file in Drive can be used in any email, campaign or post — no need to re-upload it each time.
  • Videos up to 2 GB. Use + New → Video; a percentage shows the upload's progress. Videos and PDF, PowerPoint or Word files can then be attached to LinkedIn and Instagram posts. See Videos, documents, Reels and stories.
  • Deleting affects everything using it. If an email references an image and you delete that image, the email breaks. Check before removing anything.

Still stuck? Contact support.
